analysis.one_liner: Freezes gasoline prices at their March 2003 level until the Energy Department studies price spikes.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its House committee referral and died when the 108th Congress ended without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal to sell gasoline, wholesale or retail, for more than its price in the same market on March 10, 2003. Sellers breaking the cap would owe a $10,000 fine for each day of violation. The freeze would end 60 days after the Secretary of Energy delivered a report analyzing what drives gasoline price swings, including whether price gouging plays a role, along with recommendations for stopping gouging.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy gasoline would be protected from price increases above the March 10, 2003 level for as long as the freeze was in effect, and the required Energy Department report would give Congress a public accounting of whether gouging contributes to price spikes.

how_it_helps.text: It would make it unlawful to sell gasoline at wholesale or retail above the price that grade sold for in the same market on March 10, 2003, capping prices during a period of fluctuations.
Violators would owe a civil penalty of $10,000 for each day a violation occurred, giving the cap teeth.

The freeze would last until 60 days after the Secretary of Energy reported to Congress on gasoline price fluctuations, with particular attention to price gouging as a cause, and with recommendations for actions to improve price stability and eliminate gouging.

analysis.who_pays: Gasoline producers, refiners, wholesalers, and retailers would bear the cost: any price above the March 10, 2003 baseline would become unlawful, and sellers facing higher wholesale costs in the meantime could not pass them on, risking losses or shortages if replacement costs exceeded the frozen price.

drawbacks.text: Freezing retail and wholesale prices at a single day's level while underlying costs move creates a real risk of shortages, because sellers who must pay more to restock gasoline would be barred from passing those costs on; the bill contained no cost-adjustment mechanism.

The freeze had no firm end date of its own: it expired only 60 days after the Secretary of Energy submitted the required report, so its duration depended entirely on how long the executive branch took to produce that analysis.
A flat $10,000-per-day penalty applies identically to a large refinery and a small independent station, and sellers could face penalties for prices set by market conditions outside their control.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's goal — protecting drivers from sudden price spikes while the government investigated whether gouging was behind them — addressed a real pocketbook concern. But the design was crude: a nationwide price freeze pegged to one day's price, with no mechanism for adjusting to changed supply costs, risks shortages and penalizes sellers for market movements. A temporary freeze with that risk may cost consumers more at the pump in shortages than it saves in price restraint.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, and no further action ever came before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Filner introduced the bill on March 20, 2003, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On April 10, 2003, the committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it remained without a hearing or vote for the rest of the 108th Congress.
The bill attracted one cosponsor, so support never grew beyond its sponsor and a single ally.
No further action is listed in the bill's history, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, without the bill reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gasoline refiners, wholesalers, and retailers are better off, since nothing ever constrained them from selling at whatever prices the market bore after March 2003. Consumers got neither the price cap nor the Energy Department study of price gouging the bill would have required.

for.name: Rep. Bob Filner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to freeze gasoline prices pending an Energy Department study of price fluctuations and gouging.

for.name: One Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for a hearing or vote, instead sending it to a subcommittee where it sat for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee, 108th Congress
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, held the scheduling power that determined whether the bill ever advanced; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's two supporters were both Democrats, but with no roll call there is no record of how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill would have made it unlawful to sell gasoline wholesale above its March 10, 2003 market price, blocking any pass-through of rising costs, with a $10,000-per-day penalty. Its death meant pricing stayed unrestricted.

Retail prices would have been frozen at the March 10, 2003 level, with the same per-day penalty; had costs risen above the frozen price, stations would have sold at a loss or stopped selling. The freeze never took effect, so retail pricing remained free.
